questions.q: What is the famous dictum of Zaha Hadid regarding the poetic nature of design?
o: Design should be an enclosure of simple excitement, where the person is the shelter of the space.
Architecture is a machine for living, where optimism is the primary fuel for shelter.

Architecture is how the person places herself in the space. Optimism is the cause. I don’t think that architecture is only about shelter, is only about a very simple enclosure. It should be able to excite you, to calm you, to make you think.
There are 90 degrees in every corner, so architecture must find the 361st degree to be poetic.
questions.n: This is the complete, original dictum emphasizing that architecture must go beyond mere function.

questions.q: Which building in China did Zaha Hadid design that is known for its twin-peaked, pebble-like structures?
questions.n: This building's design was inspired by pebbles in a stream smoothed by erosion, featuring two main volumes.

questions.q: What was Zaha Hadid's first major built project?
o: Vitra Fire Station (Weil am Rhein, Germany)
questions.n: Completed in 1993, this was her first major commission to be physically realized.

questions.q: Who designed the "Turning Torso" in Malmö, Sweden, inspired by a twisting human silhouette?
questions.n: An architect-engineer known for sculptural, anthropomorphic, and zoomorphic forms.

questions.q: Which architect is considered the "Father of Modernism"?
questions.n: As the mentor to Wright and pioneer of the skyscraper, he is widely regarded as the Father of Modern Architecture.

questions.q: Who is the "Father of American Architecture"?
questions.n: He developed a uniquely American style (Prairie Style) that broke away from European traditions.

questions.q: Who is the "Father of Skyscrapers"?
questions.n: He established the aesthetic and functional logic of the tall building (base, shaft, capital).

questions.q: Which architect designed the Farnsworth House, a masterpiece of the International Style?
questions.n: The house is a definitive example of his 'skin and bones' architecture.

questions.q: What is the only skyscraper designed by Frank Lloyd Wright?
questions.n: It is his only realized high-rise building, based on a 'tree' structural concept.

questions.q: Where was the original location of the Bauhaus school when it was founded by Walter Gropius?
questions.n: The school was founded here in 1919 before political pressure forced it to move.

questions.q: Which architect designed the Paimio Sanatorium and is known for his "humanistic" approach to modernism?
questions.n: His work incorporated natural materials and curved forms to create a more psychological and physical comfort.

questions.q: Which building by Frank Lloyd Wright features a workspace with "dendriform" (tree-like) concrete columns?
questions.n: The Great Workroom features high mushroom-shaped columns that support the roof.

questions.q: Who are the two primary architects who designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris?
questions.n: They won the competition with their High-Tech 'inside-out' design.

questions.q: In Egyptian architecture, what is the term for walls that are sloped or inclined inward?
questions.n: This sloping profile provided stability and became a hallmark of the Egyptian aesthetic.

questions.q: In Egyptian ornamentation, what did the Scarab represent?
questions.n: The dung beetle rolling its ball was seen as a symbol of the sun and the renewal of life.

questions.q: In Egyptian ornamentation, what did the Papyrus represent?
questions.n: As a plant from the Nile, it symbolized the abundance and life-giving properties of the river.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest church in the world, a masterpiece of Renaissance architecture in Vatican City?
questions.n: The central church of the Vatican, designed by a series of Renaissance masters.

questions.q: Who designed the revolutionary double-shelled dome of the Florence Cathedral (Sta. Maria del Fiore)?
questions.n: He solved the engineering riddle of how to vault the massive crossing without centering.

questions.q: Which architectural style is characterized by asymmetrical patterns, delicate scrolls, and pastel colors, evolving from the Late Baroque?
questions.n: It was a lighter, more decorative, and often asymmetrical style used mostly for interiors.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between Baroque and Rococo?
o: Baroque is circular; Rococo is linear.
Baroque is grand, dramatic, and heavy; Rococo is light, playful, and intimate.
Baroque uses stone; Rococo uses wood.
Baroque is European; Rococo is American.
questions.n: Baroque was the style of absolute monarchy and the Church; Rococo was for the aristocracy's private salons.

questions.q: Which Filipino architect designed the WHO (World Health Organization) Regional Headquarters in Manila?
questions.n: A pioneer of Philippine Modernism known for clean lines and functional design.

questions.q: Which building is famous for its large folded-plate canopy design?
o: SSS Main Building (designed by Juan Nakpil)
questions.n: The entrance canopy is a classic example of this structural and aesthetic form.

questions.q: Which National Artist for Architecture designed the State Theater and the Manila City Hall?
questions.n: He was a pioneer who significantly shaped the skyline of pre-war and post-war Manila.

questions.q: Who is the architect of the Capitol Theater in Manila?
questions.n: The Capitol Theater on Escolta is one of his most recognized Art Deco works.

questions.q: Which indigenous Philippine house is known for being a windowless, one-room structure elevated on four posts with "rat guards"?
questions.n: The windowless design and 'halipan' (rat guards) on the posts are unique to this highland dwelling.

questions.q: Which city hall in the Philippines is historically significant for its extensive use of wood in its original construction?
o: Cabanatuan City Hall (historical context) or Iloilo City Hall (Old).
questions.n: Many older municipal halls transitioned from wooden structures to concrete; Cabanatuan is a common board exam reference for this.

questions.q: Who designed the Magsaysay Center, one of the first buildings to use a column-free interior via a structural core?
questions.n: This building was a milestone in high-rise engineering and modernist aesthetics in the Philippines.

questions.q: What is the "Greenbelt" area in Makati often cited for in Theory of Architecture (TOA)?
o: Its integration of commercial space with lush tropical landscaping and open space.
Its status as the first high-rise in the country
questions.n: It is an example of an 'urban oasis' and successful pedestrian-centric commercial planning.

questions.q: Which architect is known for the "Butterfly" roof design in early Philippine modernism?
questions.n: His residential works often featured the clean, upward-sloping planes of the butterfly roof.

questions.q: What is the traditional meaning of the "Feather" in Egyptian art/architecture?
questions.n: The heart of the deceased was weighed against this feather to determine their worthiness for the afterlife.

questions.q: What is Section 33 of RA 9266?
o: Ownership of Plans, Specifications, and other Contract Documents.
questions.n: It protects the architect's work as their intellectual property.

questions.q: Under RA 9266, do architectural plans remain the property of the architect even after the project is finished and paid for?
o: Yes, but only if the project is never built.
No, they become public property after 10 years.
No, they belong to the client once fully paid.
Yes, the copyright and intellectual property remain with the architect.
questions.n: The law explicitly states that plans are instruments of service and remain the property of the author.

questions.q: Which SPP document covers Pre-Design Services?
questions.n: This covers services like feasibility studies and site analysis before actual design begins.

questions.q: Which SPP document covers Regular Design Services?
questions.n: This covers the standard 5-6 phases of project design and construction.

questions.q: Which SPP document covers Post-Construction Services?
questions.n: Covers building management, maintenance, and post-occupancy evaluation.

questions.q: Under SPP 205, how is the architect typically compensated for managing a building's maintenance and operations?
o: Free of charge as part of the original design contract.
Percentage of gross rentals or a fixed monthly fee.
Multiple of direct personnel expenses only.
A percentage of the project construction cost (PCC).
questions.n: Since the service is ongoing and operational, the fee is linked to the building's income or a set management rate.

questions.q: In Regular Design Services (202), what is the percentage of the architect's fee due upon the completion of the Schematic Design Phase?
questions.n: This is the cumulative percentage due after the first design phase.

questions.q: In Regular Design Services (202), what is the percentage due after the Contract Document Phase?
questions.n: This phase alone is 50%, which brings the total cumulative payment to 85%.

questions.q: What is the method of compensation where the architect is paid for actual hours spent plus a multiplier?
questions.n: Commonly used for non-creative work or as a basis for other fee types.

questions.q: What is a "Lump Sum" fee?
o: A fixed amount agreed upon for a specific scope of work, regardless of the final construction cost.
A fee that is paid only at the end of the project.
A fee based on the weight of the blueprints.
A fee that increases automatically with inflation.
questions.n: Provides cost certainty for the client but risk for the architect if scope creeps.

questions.q: What type of permit is required specifically for the construction of a swimming pool?
questions.n: Used for structures that are secondary to the main building, like pools, fences, and towers.

questions.q: Which type of permits are issued by the Building Official for parts of the building like electronics, mechanical, or plumbing?
questions.n: These are the technical sub-permits that complete the building permit application.

questions.q: What is an "Easement" in urban areas?
o: A tax levied on large property owners.
The public space between the property line and the curb, intended for public use and utilities.
The maximum height a building can reach.
The area where a building is allowed to stand.
questions.n: It is a right of way provided for the benefit of the community and public infrastructure.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an "Agricultural Easement"?
o: To protect water bodies (rivers/creeks) from encroachment and pollution, usually requiring a wider clearance (20m).
To provide space for tractors to turn.
To ensure every farm has a road.
To allow neighbors to graze their cattle.
questions.n: Larger easements are required in agricultural areas to prevent runoff and ecological damage.

questions.q: What is the required easement for an urban area (residential/commercial) along a waterway?
questions.n: The minimum requirement for developed urban environments.

questions.q: What is the required easement for a forest area along a waterway?
questions.n: Forest zones require the widest protection to preserve the natural ecosystem.

questions.q: What is the required easement for an agricultural area along a waterway?
questions.n: This is the standard buffer for agricultural lands.

questions.q: Are "Traditional Indigenous Family Dwellings" (like a Bahay Kubo) with a construction cost not exceeding 15,000 PHP exempted from building permit fees?
o: Yes, but only if they are made of stone.
No, they are only exempt from electrical permits.
No, all structures must pay fees.
questions.n: The National Building Code provides exemptions for traditional dwellings below this cost threshold to assist low-income families.

questions.q: What is the specific code for the National Plumbing Code of the Philippines?
questions.n: The law that regulates the practice of master plumbing and sanitation standards.

questions.q: What is the specific code for the Fire Code of the Philippines?
questions.n: The current and comprehensive law for fire safety in the Philippines.
